Results

VTEMajors2026. Enoxaparin and unfractionated heparin prophylaxis.

Rebuilt from VTE cleaned data.xlsx, Sheet1, on 30 September 2026 at 20:35 AEST. All analyses were performed in R.

PopulationTreatmentOutcomesTime to VTEAdjusted modelsSmokingDosesAppendices

Study population and baseline characteristics

The analysis included 713 records with distinct study identifiers, comprising 487 enoxaparin records and 226 UFH records. Recorded weight ranged from 120 to 382 kg, and age ranged from 17 to 97 years. Treatment and outcome flags were complete.

Median age was 52.0 (41.0 to 62.0) years with enoxaparin and 53.0 (42.0 to 63.0) years with UFH. Median weight was 144.6 (132.0 to 165.0) kg and 134.9 (125.2 to 151.0) kg, respectively. Median recorded eGFR was 88.0 (68.2 to 90.0) with enoxaparin and 80.0 (54.0 to 90.0) with UFH. Values in parentheses are interquartile ranges.

Cancer was recorded in 50 (10.3%) of the enoxaparin group and 54 (23.9%) of the UFH group. Surgery before or at prophylaxis initiation was recorded in 86 (17.7%) and 65 (28.8%), respectively.

Treatment and admission characteristics

Median prophylaxis duration was 5.0 (3.0 to 9.0) days with enoxaparin and 6.5 (4.0 to 11.0) days with UFH. A positive missed-dose entry was recorded in 233 (47.8%) and 195 (86.3%), respectively. Weight-based prescribing was flagged in 19 records, all in the enoxaparin group.

The missed-dose field contains mixed apparent scales. Only the presence of a positive entry is compared. This measure depends on exposure duration and scheduled administrations and does not estimate an adherence rate. Treatment-course variables were excluded from baseline adjustment models.

VTE, recorded bleeding and haemoglobin drop

VTE occurred in 4/487 enoxaparin records (0.8%) and 13/226 UFH records (5.8%). The risk difference was -4.93 percentage points (95% CI -8.80 to -2.25), and the risk ratio was 0.14 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.43). Fisher exact p <0.001.

Recorded bleed occurred in 9/487 enoxaparin records (1.8%) and 6/226 UFH records (2.7%). The risk difference was -0.81 percentage points (95% CI -3.95 to 1.36), and the risk ratio was 0.70 (95% CI 0.25 to 1.93). Fisher exact p = 0.576.

Haemoglobin drop occurred in 15/487 enoxaparin records (3.1%) and 28/226 UFH records (12.4%). The risk difference was -9.31 percentage points (95% CI -14.39 to -5.15), and the risk ratio was 0.25 (95% CI 0.14 to 0.46). Fisher exact p <0.001.

The bleeding confidence interval remains compatible with both lower and higher risk.

Time to VTE during prophylaxis

All 713 records contributed usable follow-up, with 17 VTE events over 8,551 prophylaxis-days. Enoxaparin contributed 6029 days and UFH contributed 2522 days. Follow-up began at prophylaxis initiation and ended at VTE or prophylaxis cessation.

The unadjusted enoxaparin-versus-UFH hazard ratio was 0.160 (95% CI 0.052 to 0.494), p = 0.001. The log-rank comparison gave p <0.001.

Figure 1. VTE-free survival during the first 30 prophylaxis days

At day 30, 30 enoxaparin and 14 UFH records remained at risk. The last VTE occurred at day 85, when only 3 UFH records remained at risk. Full follow-up estimates and sensitivity analyses are provided in the appendix.

Curves use the full recorded follow-up, displayed to day 30. Dashed lines are pointwise 95% confidence intervals and crosses denote censoring. These estimates apply to the observed prophylaxis course. Death and other cessation reasons were unavailable, so independent censoring cannot be verified and competing-risk incidence was not estimated.

Adjusted VTE comparisons

Adjustment for cancer and surgery yielded a hazard ratio of 0.159 (95% CI 0.051 to 0.500), p = 0.002. Adding continuous age and sex gave a hazard ratio of 0.191 (95% CI 0.061 to 0.600), p = 0.005. All models included the same 713 records and 17 events.

Table 5. Enoxaparin versus UFH across the fitted Cox models

ModelRecordsVTE eventsHazard ratio (95% CI)Wald p
Unadjusted713170.160 (0.052 to 0.494)0.001
Cancer and surgery713170.159 (0.051 to 0.500)0.002
Exploratory: add age and sex713170.191 (0.061 to 0.600)0.005
Cancer, surgery and smoking code713170.178 (0.056 to 0.566)0.003

The core model estimated three coefficients and the age-and-sex model estimated five. Only 1 VTE event occurred in a female record. The global proportional-hazards diagnostic gave p = 0.095 for the core model and p = 0.009 for the age-and-sex model. Surgery-specific diagnostic p values were 0.050 and 0.001, respectively. The expanded model is therefore presented as exploratory.

The adjustment sequence was specified during analysis discussions after descriptive results were available. Surgery was confirmed to precede or coincide with prophylaxis initiation. Cancer was treated as a baseline clinical characteristic. These models do not establish a causal treatment effect, and renal function remains a potential source of residual confounding.

Smoking sensitivity analysis

Smoking data were available for all 713 records included in the sensitivity analysis. Adding smoking code to the cancer-and-surgery model yielded an enoxaparin-versus-UFH HR of 0.178 (95% CI 0.056 to 0.566, p = 0.003), compared with 0.159 (95% CI 0.051 to 0.500) in the same-cohort model without smoking. The Firth estimate after smoking adjustment was 0.194 (95% CI 0.057 to 0.553).

The smoking-adjusted model's global proportional-hazards test gave p = 0.309. The corresponding smoking-factor test gave p = 0.377, and surgery gave p = 0.117. No convergence warnings were recorded. The model remains limited by sparse events, provisional smoking definitions and possible residual confounding. These diagnostic tests have limited power with few events. Firth estimation does not resolve non-proportional hazards or informative cessation.

Smoking was included as a three-level factor with N as reference. Y and X remained separate categories. The definitions of N, Y and X and their baseline recording have not been confirmed, so category-specific effects are labelled by source code. The sensitivity analysis assumes these codes describe status at prophylaxis initiation. It adds smoking to cancer and surgery and does not also include age and sex.

Exploratory dose comparisons within each drug

For Enoxaparin, the comparison of 80 versus 40 mg/day included 391 of 487 records. There were 0 VTE events over 3681 prophylaxis-days at the higher total and 2 over 863 days at the lower total. The unadjusted rate ratio was 0.000 (95% CI 0.000 to 1.248, exact p = 0.072, Holm-adjusted p = 0.433).

For UFH, the comparison of 15000 versus 10000 units/day included 221 of 226 records. There were 11 VTE events over 1918 prophylaxis-days at the higher total and 2 over 590 days at the lower total. The unadjusted rate ratio was 1.692 (95% CI 0.369 to 15.708, exact p = 0.758, Holm-adjusted p = 1.000).

The selected enoxaparin comparison included 2 of 4 enoxaparin VTE events. The remaining enoxaparin events occurred at other recorded daily totals. No adjusted dose-effect model was fitted.

Dose categories are recorded daily totals. Administration frequency, baseline regimen, changes during therapy, renal dose adjustments and time at each regimen were unavailable. Prophylaxis-days are attributed to the recorded total for these exploratory summaries. Dose comparisons are unadjusted and can reflect differences in patient selection, duration or dose recording. A zero event count gives a boundary rate-ratio estimate and does not establish a protective effect. Bleeding and Hb-drop comparisons use recorded outcome flags, with the timing limitations described in the data checks. No adjusted dose-effect model was fitted because of the sparse events and incomplete regimen information.

Statistical and data-quality appendices

Distribution assessment and normality tests

Distribution checks comprised histograms, normal Q-Q plots and Shapiro-Wilk tests within each drug group. Shapiro-Wilk p values were below 0.05 for 9 of 10 baseline variable-by-group distributions and 4 of 4 therapy-duration and length-of-stay distributions (13 of 14 overall). Continuous characteristics are summarised using medians and interquartile ranges, with Wilcoxon rank-sum comparisons. The plots and clinical measurement scales guide that reporting choice alongside the test results. Wilcoxon comparisons assess rank distributions and do not, in general, test a difference in medians alone. Mean, standard deviation, range, missingness and sample skewness are provided in the descriptive appendix. These diagnostic p values are unadjusted and are not study-outcome hypothesis tests.

Firth estimates use a penalty of 0.5 with profile penalised-likelihood intervals and tests. Conventional Breslow estimates distinguish tie-handling effects from penalisation. The post hoc stratified model has separate baseline hazards for surgery/sex combinations and a common drug coefficient. Eventless strata contribute no event comparisons. These sensitivity analyses do not resolve residual confounding, informative cessation or sparse information.

All source rows were retained in the main analyses. Age categories were derived from numeric age. Non-events have structurally missing event times. Hb-drop events with missing timing remain in the outcome counts. The workbook does not establish repeated admissions, treatment switches, prophylaxis gaps, death or reasons for cessation. Each row is treated as an independent record.

Statistical methods and reproducibility

Continuous summaries use R type 7 quartiles. Normality was assessed with Shapiro-Wilk tests and histogram/Q-Q plots within each treatment group. Wilcoxon tests use the normal approximation with continuity correction. Categorical tests use Pearson chi-square without continuity correction when all expected counts are at least five, otherwise Fisher exact. All tests are two-sided. No automatic variable selection was used.

Between-drug risk differences use Newcombe intervals combining Wilson scores. Risk-ratio intervals use the log-Wald method without continuity correction. Kaplan-Meier intervals use log-log transformation. Cox models use Efron ties and Wald intervals unless stated otherwise. The cancer-and-surgery, age-and-sex and smoking models used the same complete cohort. Covariate selection was informed by clinical discussion during the analysis phase.

Smoking was entered as a three-level factor with N as the reference. The source labels N, Y and X are retained because their clinical definitions have not been confirmed. The smoking model included drug, cancer and baseline surgery and estimated five coefficients from 17 events. Conventional Cox models used Efron ties, with Wald confidence intervals and tests. Firth models used a penalty of 0.5, Breslow ties and profile penalised-likelihood confidence intervals and tests. Conventional Breslow models separate tie-handling differences from penalisation.

The two most common recorded daily totals within each drug were compared after inspection of the data. These post hoc comparisons were 80 versus 40 mg/day for enoxaparin and 15,000 versus 10,000 units/day for UFH. Other recorded totals remain in the descriptive tables and were excluded only from these pairwise comparisons. Risk confidence intervals are two-sided Clopper-Pearson intervals. VTE rates use exact Poisson confidence intervals. Rate ratios use conditional equal-tailed exact confidence intervals with central two-sided p values calculated as twice the smaller binomial tail, capped at one. Poisson comparisons assume independent event counts with the specified person-time exposures and a constant rate within each group. Risk differences use Newcombe intervals from Wilson scores without continuity correction. Bleed and Hb-drop risk comparisons use two-sided Fisher exact tests. VTE risk differences are descriptive without a duplicate hypothesis test. The six selected dose tests, comprising two VTE rate tests and four bleed or Hb-drop risk tests, are reported with both nominal and Holm-adjusted p values. Confidence intervals are pointwise 95% intervals.

The source workbook was unchanged, verified using MD5 4143a5186394641e51c1102e936c394a. This run used R version 4.3.3 (2024-02-29), readxl 1.4.5, survival 3.5.8, coxphf 1.13.4, ragg 1.3.2 and base64enc 0.1.3. Full_R_output.txt records the run and session information.

Reproduce the analysis by sourcing VTEMajors2026_step_by_step.R. The numbered sections start with the Excel import. VTE_helpers.R contains the commented reusable calculations. VTE_report.R renders this Results section from the new analysis objects. No exported result tables are reused as analysis inputs.

Methods references: Shapiro-Wilk, exact Poisson intervals, Cox models, proportional-hazards diagnostics, Firth Cox estimation, Newcombe risk differences, and observational comparative-effects methods.
